long.description:
How did 400 strangers bring down the greatest city the Americas had ever seen? This is the story of Tenochtitlan — and it has haunted me since I first stood where its temples once rose.

In 1519, Hernán Cortés marched into a floating metropolis of 200,000 people — bigger than London, richer than Seville. Within two years, it was starved, burned, and erased. This is the Night of Sorrows, the 93-day siege, the invisible killer that did what no army could, and the last emperor who refused to kneel.

CHAPTERS:
0:03 The Eagle Falls
0:38 The Floating City
1:31 Omens in the Sky
1:56 The Strangers Land
2:32 The Welcome
3:06 Blood in the Temple
3:38 La Noche Triste
4:38 The Invisible Killer
5:16 The Gathering Storm
5:57 Ninety-Three Days
6:54 August 13, 1521
7:47 What Remains
8:23 Echoes

What stays with me is not the conquest — it's the city itself. A metropolis on water, feeding hundreds of thousands, built by people Europe called savages. If you love epic stories from world history, subscribe to Echoes of History Channel for a new documentary every day.

shorts.description:
On August 13, 1521, the largest city on the planet fell silent. Tenochtitlan — a floating metropolis of 300,000 souls — lay starved and broken. How did 400 strangers destroy the greatest empire the Americas had ever known?

Watch the full story on Echoes of History Channel.
shorts.title: The Greatest City on Earth Vanished in 93 Days

shorts.description:
On the Night of Sorrows, the Spaniards fled Tenochtitlan with gold sewn into their clothes. Weighed down by greed, they slipped from the bridges and drowned in the lake.

Watch the full story on Echoes of History Channel.
shorts.title: They Sewed Gold Into Their Clothes — Then Drowned

shorts.description:
Smallpox reached Tenochtitlan before Cortés did. With no immunity and no cure, it emptied the greatest city in the Americas faster than any army ever could.

Watch the full story on Echoes of History Channel.
shorts.title: A Disease Killed More Aztecs Than Any Sword
